name: Trade Way — Travellers on the Road
description: Roadside strangers on the Trade Way, south of Daggerford toward the Misty Forest — non-combat, roleplay travel encounters. NONE of these travellers know the village of Greenrest or the party's true quest. Two entries — the trapper (05) and the minstrel's ballad (07) — carry a very nascent, deniable clue to the hidden plot; let them pass as woodsman's superstition and an old sad song. Rollable on any leg of the journey.

results.description: Ordella Vance & caravan — a northbound merchant train, three wagons of Daggerford cloth and tin, guards riding drag. The master, a broad, tired woman, hails the party for road-news and to warn them off the southern stretches: “Not bandit-quiet down there. Empty-quiet. Didn't pass a living soul in two days. You mind yourselves.” Glad to trade rations or gossip.

Brother Tobin — a barefoot hedge-priest of Chauntea, sunburned and dusty, walking a circuit of roadside shrines. He blesses the party's journey unasked and lingers to talk weather and crops. “The Lady's been strange with her gifts of late — some fields simply cannot fail, others starve a mile off. She doesn't usually play favourites.” He means nothing by it.
GM — gives the party: @UUID[Item.pHpBTpv3LIbYBaq7]{Chauntea's Barley-Token} — a Chauntea blessing-token he presses on them as he goes.

Denby Cobble — a peddler and his put-upon mule, cart jangling with pans, ribbons, and dubious charms. Relentlessly cheerful; he'll try to sell the party a “genuine feywood luck-knot, blessed and everything” for a silver, and throw in three tall tales for free. Utterly harmless.
GM — gives the party: @UUID[Item.H98ptfXZplBOFX25]{Feywood Luck-Knot} — if they buy it (a silver) or just humour him, the charm is a real keepsake.

Corwin Vale — a traveller in mourning grey, carrying a small wrapped bundle he will not set down. Courteous and quiet, bound south to bury his wife where the two were wed. If the party is kind he says, softly: “They tell you grief passes. It doesn't. It just learns to walk beside you.” Then he tips his head and walks on.

Halgar Vos — a trapper coming out of the deep woods; furs, a bad limp, eyes on everything. He'll swap pelts for salt and steel. The warn-you-off sort: “That old wood's fey country, and fey country don't keep our clock. A thing down there'll wait a hundred years for someone who's never coming back — they don't understand ending. Don't stay long enough to catch it.”
GM — nascent clue: the fey inability to accept a death. To him it's pure woodsman's superstition; let it pass unremarked.

Pib & Josk — two couriers on lathered horses, racing the same sealed letter to two rival lords, each loudly certain the other is a forger and a scoundrel. They'll actually pay the party to arbitrate — then gallop off still bellowing, the argument entirely unresolved.

Marisel — a wandering minstrel with a road-worn lute, glad of any audience; she plays for a coin or a hot meal. Deep in her repertoire is a very old, half-forgotten ballad — “The Green and the Grey” — about a deathless green thing that loved a mortal youth and could not let him go when his years ran out. A sad old tune, she thinks, nothing more. Asked the youth's name, the oldest verse gives only “Corin.”
GM — nascent clue: a garbled folk-memory of the Dreamer and Corin. The minstrel has no idea it's true; don't let her tie it to any place.
GM — gives the party: @UUID[Item.R8Ht21MSdnajwZKw]{Ballad Sheet: The Green and the Grey} — for a coin or a kindness she'll write the ballad's words out (the handout that names Corin).

Weslo Crane — a self-appointed “road-warden” at a rickety poled barrier, a weaselly man in a too-large tabard who insists the Trade Way now carries a toll, payable to him, for “upkeep and protection.” There is no upkeep and no protection; he folds the instant he's challenged. (Quiet foreshadowing: the next thing on this road that wants a toll won't be bluffing.)

Rurik Dunn — a lone survivor of another expedition, gear half-gone and flinching at shadows, hurrying north. Whatever they went south for, he won't say — only: “Whatever's on your map, it isn't worth the crossing. We were six.” Can't be talked into turning back. A ready drop-in ally, or a grim omen — GM's choice.

Mother Ziska — an old fortune-teller in a mule-drawn wagon strung with charms, who offers to read the party's road for a coin. Her patter is cold-reading and cheap mystery — but she's uncannily good at it. She sends them off with something that sounds like a warning and means nothing yet: “Green roads ahead of you. Mind you don't fall asleep on them.”
GM — gives the party: @UUID[Item.DZPWN8w4xxhYZElr]{Mother Ziska's Fortune Card} — the card she deals them at the end of the reading.

The Harrow family — settlers heading north (father Tam, a laden handcart, a lean dog, three quiet children), giving up on a southern holding that never quite took. Weary but decent; they'll share a fire and a thin stew. “Land looked fine. Just never felt like ours. Some places don't want keeping.”

Nell & Gorm Alder — two old pilgrims married some forty years, walking a shrine circuit hand in hand and finishing each other's sentences. Sweet, funny, endlessly hospitable — they'll press food on the party and dispense unsolicited wisdom on love, feet, and weather. A small bright picture of a whole mortal life, freely given.
GM — gives the party: @UUID[Item.EXO8oHOZp3hAv5cO]{Pilgrim's Shrine-Token} — a little shrine-token pressed on them with their blessing.
